title: Leader-Based Read Path
summary:
The read path is about **where a read is served and how fresh it must be**. Only the leader is guaranteed to have all committed writes, but every read on the leader uses the capacity that writes need.

Routing options:

- **Read from the leader:** fresh, but it limits read throughput.
- **Read from a follower:** scales reads, but the data may be stale by the replication lag.
- **Route by need:** reads that feed a decision or follow the user's own write go to the leader (or to a follower that has caught up); everything else goes to followers.

Techniques:

- **Position-tagged reads:** a write returns its log position; the next read goes to a follower only if its applied position is at least that, or else waits or falls back to the leader.
- **Lag-aware routing:** remove followers whose lag exceeds a threshold from the read pool.
- **Sticky routing:** keep one user on the same follower so reads do not go backward in time.
- **Reading from the leader is not automatically fresh:** a deposed leader that does not know it was replaced can serve stale reads, so linear reads need a leadership check (a [lease](#/sd/f/lease) or a quorum round).

Which guarantees these give are formalised in [leader-based consistency](#/sd/f/leader-based-consistency); the write side is in the [write path](#/sd/f/leader-based-write-path). A [read/write replica split](#/sd/f/rw-replicas) is the common deployment.

drills.q: A shopping app serves reads from followers. Which reads should still go to the leader (or a caught-up replica)? Select all that apply.
options: Showing a customer their order immediately after they place it
The balance check inside a transaction that decides whether to allow a withdrawal
drills.explain: Read-your-own-writes and reads that feed a write decision must not be stale. Catalog browsing and analytics tolerate lag, and they are the bulk of traffic, which is why they are the reads you move to followers.

drills.q: A single node serves at most 5,000 reads/s. The workload is 18,000 reads/s, and the leader serves no reads. Each follower counts as one node. What is the minimum number of followers needed?
drills.explain: 18,000 / 5,000 = 3.6, so 4 followers (4 x 5,000 = 20,000). Three followers would be saturated at 15,000/s, with no headroom for failures or spikes, which in practice means you need more than the minimum.

drills.q: The router measures follower lag as 8 s on follower F2 while your freshness budget is 2 s. What should it do?
options: Take F2 out of the read pool until its lag recovers, sending its reads to other followers (or the leader)
Keep routing, because eventual consistency covers it
Retry the same read on F2 until it is fresh
drills.explain: A budget is only meaningful if it is enforced by routing. Make sure the remaining pool can take the load; if every follower lags, fall back to the leader or shed load rather than serving data that breaks the guarantee.

drills.q: An old leader is partitioned from the rest of the cluster; a new leader has been elected. A client that still reaches the old leader reads from it. Is the data fresh?
options: Not necessarily: the old leader may still believe it is the leader and serve stale reads, so it must confirm leadership via a lease or quorum before answering
Yes, the leader always has the latest data
Yes, if the read is a primary key lookup
No, because leaders never serve reads
drills.explain: 'Read from the leader' is only fresh while it really is the leader. Lease-based leadership (the leader stops serving when its lease lapses) or a quorum check on each read closes that gap; see failover for the write-side analogue.

drills.q: Order the steps of a position-tagged read-your-writes read.
items: The write commits at log position 1042 and the client stores 1042
The client issues a read with min_position = 1042
The router picks a follower and checks its applied position
If the follower is at or beyond 1042 it serves the read
Otherwise the read waits briefly or is redirected to the leader
drills.explain: The token carries the causal dependency, so the system only pays the leader read cost when a follower is actually behind. A fixed 'read from the leader for N seconds' rule is simpler but coarser.

drills.q: List three read-routing policies for a leader-based store and the staleness each one allows.
drills.answer: Leader-only (none, but limited read capacity); any follower (stale by the replication lag, can go backward between followers); lag- or position-aware routing (bounded staleness or read-your-writes, at the price of a position check and a fallback to the leader).
